claims.claim_text: Wallach calls red meat an unequaled source of animal protein and essential lipids; the only trick is to cook it no more than medium, since well-done or burnt fat forms heterocyclic amines. He even recommends raw steak tartare.
claims.verbatim:
Red meat is an unequaled source of animal protein and essential 
lipids - the secret is to not eat meat cooked well done or eat the fat 
burnt as they become heterocyclic amines. Medium rare and me- 
dium are the safe way to eat beef. Steak Tartar is a half pound of raw, 
freshly ground sirloin, served with chopped onions, pepper corns 
and topped with a raw egg - it doesn’t get any better than this!

claims.claim_text: Wallach cites a 930-woman study where eating beef and pork very well done raised breast-cancer risk 462% versus medium-rare; his point is that it is not the fat but the cooking that harms you, because burnt animal fat becomes heterocyclic amines, powerful carcinogens.
claims.verbatim:
On November 18, 1998, Dr. Wei Zheng of the University of South 
Carolina reported that in a study of 930 women, those who ate their 
beef and pork cooked very well done increased their risk of breast 
cancer by 462 percent over those women who ate their meat cooked 
medium rare - it is not the amount of fat in the diet that counts, but 
rather, how you cook the fat that counts. Burnt animal fat is con- 
verted to heterocyclic amines which are extremely powerful carcino- 
gens.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's 'Feedlot Syndrome' analogy: ranchers fatten beef cattle on a steady stream of carbohydrate feed paired with optimal nutrients that drive the animal to eat with endless, fervent hunger, growing a 40-lb calf to 900-1,100 lb in a year. He argues humans are fattened by the same carb-heavy diet — but, unlike the optimally-supplemented cattle, humans eat it while mineral-deficient, which is what leaves them with a ravenous appetite.
claims.verbatim:
Raising prime beef successfully, requires a steady stream of car- 
bohydrate, protein and fat calories in the proper ratios specifically 
designed for fattening. 
The intense weight gain, high carbohydrate diet must be accom- 
panied by optimal mixes of nutrients designed to encourage weight 
gain and drive the animal to eat with an endless and fervent hunger. 
Feed, based on corn or other carbohydrates, is made available in 
a steady stream. Beef cattle will grow from a forty pound calf to 900 
- 1,100 pounds in about a year under optimal feedlot conditions.

claims.claim_text: Not on its own, in Wallach's view. He points to the Old Order Amish, who eat pork, beef, goat and mutton 3 times a day plus heavy whole milk, butter and cheese — by his account consuming more sugar, fat, red meat and dairy than anyone in North America — and yet post an obesity rate of just 4% and a type-II diabetes rate of just 6%, only about a tenth and a half, respectively, of their 'modern' neighbors in the very same county. He credits that gap not to their meat-heavy diet, and not even to their hard farm labor (the horses do most of the work), but to the essential minerals in the wood ashes they spread on their garden soil every single morning.

Wallach cites a Scientific American longevity summary: the patients who followed doctors' advice to the letter didn't reach 100, while the 'rebellious' ones who ate salt, eggs, red meat, butter and chicken skin did.
claims.verbatim:
the individuals who followed their doctors advice to the 
letter, didn’t make it to 100 years of age, while people who ate salt, 
eggs, red meat, butter and chicken skin did.

claims.claim_text: Pellagra turned out to be a dietary deficiency disease — a lack of vitamin B3 (niacin) — and eggs were part of the fix. Wallach recounts how a U.S. Public Health Service researcher noticed that in orphanages and mental asylums the residents came down with pellagra while the staff, who ate a wider variety of food, stayed well. When eggs and milk were simply added to the sufferers' diets, the pellagra disappeared. Wallach lays out the competing theories of the era — the main one blamed the limited corn diet, while some held that pellagra was an insect-borne disease like malaria or yellow fever, and sufferers were isolated in federal centers as though they were contagious like tuberculosis — and this is his illustration that nutrient-dense foods like eggs can reverse a 'disease' that was really malnutrition.
claims.verbatim:
When eggs and milk were 
added to the diet of the affected individuals, pellagra disappeared.

claims.claim_text: Yes — and it was more than a footnote. Wallach was a co-petitioner on the FDA petition (Docket No. 03Q-0401, filed 6/23/2003) that won the qualified health claim linking omega-3 fatty acids to reduced coronary heart disease risk, which the FDA allowed on 9/8/2004. It matters because it was one front in Wallach's larger legal war against the FDA — waged with First Amendment attorney Jonathan Emord — to force the agency to let supplement makers state health benefits that were actually proven. The same campaign carried his solo selenium-and-cancer claim (approved 4/28/2003); as he tells it, after losing every battle before the 1994 DSHEA Act, his side won every one that followed. So the official omega-3 heart-health language products can now use is partly his doing.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's maintenance dose for the liquid plant-derived colloidal minerals: one ounce per 100 pounds of body weight per day, ideally split. A 100-pound person takes one ounce a day (or half an ounce — one tablespoon — twice daily); a 200-pound person, two ounces; a 300-pound person, three, and so on. He specifies the supplement should carry at least 77 minerals at a concentration of 19,000 mg per quart and cover all 90 essential nutrients. For anyone needing to lose 25 pounds or more, the level can be raised to one and one-quarter ounces per 100 pounds.
claims.verbatim:
These liquid minerals should be taken at the rate of one ounce 
per hundred pounds of body weight as a maintenance dose.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's tactic for sugar cravings and the munchies while quitting sugar: take one ounce of plant-derived colloidal minerals per 100 pounds of body weight — even up to ten times a day at first. He reads cravings and pica as a sure sign of mineral deficiency, so flooding the body with absorbable minerals is meant to switch the urge off.
claims.verbatim:
If during the process of giving up sugar you get the “munchies” 
or feel the need to go on the classic “chocoholic” binge, take one 
ounce of plant derived colloidal minerals per 100 pounds of body 
weight - even if it’s ten times per day at the start (remember - cravings 
or pica are the sure sign of mineral deficiencies!!).

claims.claim_text: A practical use for the liquid complex: distilled water is mineral-free and over time pulls minerals out of the body, so Wallach suggests re-mineralizing it — add one ounce of liquid colloidal minerals (at 19,000 mg of minerals per quart) to each gallon of distilled or double-filtered water.
claims.verbatim:
A good compromise is to use distilled or double filtered water 
that has been “enriched” with liquid colloidal minerals at the rate of 
one ounce of the liquid colloidal minerals (19,000 mg of minerals 
per quart) per gallon of distilled or double filtered water.

claims.claim_text: Wallach's own outcome evidence for the complex, from a 2004 pilot study he co-authored among the Nez Perce of Idaho (Wallach, MacCoy, Henry, and Schrauzer). On a plant-derived colloidal mineral program — framed as replacing the wood ashes the tribe historically got their minerals from — almost all participants lost weight, significantly lowered their blood pressure, and cut fasting blood sugar by thirty to fifty percent, with everyone able to significantly reduce or come off their medication.
claims.verbatim:
A 2004 pilot supplement study (Wallach, J.D., MacCoy, B., Henry, 
L. and Schrauzer, G.N.) with the Nez Perce Indians of Idaho, has 
shown that almost all participants lost weight, significantly reduced 
blood pressure and reduced fasting blood sugars by thirty to fifty 
percent. All were able to significantly reduce or wean off of their 
medication.
